reason: In 'inflorescence lax-flowered' the bearer is the inflorescence, which the statement already names, and PATO loose (PATO_0001802; related synonym lax) is exactly right. Accepted siblings use the same mapping: laxly, laxiflorous and laxly arranged all go to loose. The flowers are not the bearer.

The PATO definition of bitter (PATO_0002474) is literally 'an acrid, sharp, or disagreeable flavor', so acrid taste of sap, tubers or leaves is covered. There is no pungent class in PATO or FLOPO. 'Acrid smell' would be odorous (PATO_0001331), but a part-name constraint cannot catch that, and it is rare.

'Flowers in glomerules' means flowers in dense clusters, often sessile and axillary (Amaranthaceae, Urticaceae). These are not heads on a shortened inflorescence axis, which is what FLOPO capitate requires. The accepted rule R0233 maps glomerate to PATO aggregated (exact synonym 'clustered'), the parent of capitate. The PO synonym glomerule on compound capitulum (PO_0030122) is the Asteraceae sense and does not fit general use.

Tapered size (PATO_0005015) is a size gradient along a set of parts: 'leaves decreasing upwards', 'pinnae decreasing towards the base'. On other bearers 'decreasing' can mean decreasing in number or in some other quality, so keep it to serial leaf-like parts.

Whatever follows the fragment ('to the base', 'to the middle', 'to the midrib'), the part is divided, so PATO split (PATO_0001786, 'divided into parts or divisions') is true in every reading. The depth is lost, as other kept rules lose a modifier. Parted (FLOPO_0991234) would be wrong for 'almost to the middle'.

Marine plants (seagrasses, marine herbs) grow submerged in sea water, which FLOPO aquatic (FLOPO_0991112) covers: growing wholly or partly in water. Salinity is a habitat detail outside PATO's scope, and no saline class exists. Aquatic is a correct broader term, not a wrong one.

This uses the same pattern as the accepted rule R0023 (dichasial maps to cyme inflorescence present). PO lists cincinni, scorpioid and monochasium as synonyms of cincinnus inflorescence (PO_0030132), so 'cymes cincinnate' names that inflorescence type. The word only occurs with inflorescences, so a part constraint adds nothing.

For veins, 'ill-defined' means faint or not clearly visible, which is inconspicuous (PATO_0000464), as the accepted rule maps 'obscurely veined' to inconspicuous. For margins, zones and inflorescences it means 'not sharply delimited', which inconspicuous does not cover and no class does.

Glandular-pubescent (FLOPO_0991173) requires short soft hairs, but pilose means long hairs, so the rule is wrong. No glandular-pilose class exists. Pilose (FLOPO_0991048) alone would lose the glands, and glandular (PATO_0002117) alone would lose the hair type. It needs a new class or two separate annotations, not this rule.

'Fully developed' is mostly a stage word ('fully developed leaves/fruits'), which belongs to the stage pattern, not to a quality. Only occasionally does it contrast with a reduced staminode. 'Not vestigial' is not what the text says.

The core quality is sheathing (FLOPO_0991105). 'Long' only grades the length of the sheath, like 'high' in high-conic (R1762) and 'erect' in erect-appressed (R0673), both kept. The sheath length can be recorded as its own measure.

Subterranean (FLOPO_0991035) is right for organs buried in soil, and for fruits in geocarpic species such as Arachis. 'Seeds buried in pulp', 'stomata buried' and 'glands buried in tissue' are not subterranean, so limit the rule to soil organs.

PO defines keel (PO_0025327) as the two lowest petals of a papilionaceous corolla. A pea-like flower or corolla is papilionaceous, so 'keel present' carries that type. 'Fruit pea-like' (pea-sized) and 'seed pea-like' do not, so limit the rule to flowers and corollas.

FLOPO virgate (FLOPO_0991038) has 'broom-like' as a synonym and fits plants, stems and branches with many slender erect twigs. This matches the sibling rule R0819 (broom-like, limited to whole plant|plant|shrub|habit). The corona-appendage use is not virgate.

Keep the rule as a negation, but negate dehiscent ('opening at maturity to release its contents'): a fruit 'not splitting' does not open. PATO split (PATO_0001786) is a cut or cleft shape, which is a different character, so 'not split' is wrong.
A low-conic stylopodium or operculum is still cone-shaped. 'Low' only grades the height, as 'high' does in the accepted rule high-conic maps to conical (R1762). Conical (PATO_0002021) is right.

Setulose means bearing small stiff bristles, but glandular-pubescent (FLOPO_0991173) means soft hairs, so the rule is wrong. No glandular-setulose class exists. Setose (PATO_0002289) would lose the glands and glandular (PATO_0002117) would lose the bristles.

This matches the accepted rule R0868 (multiveined maps to vascular bundle present) and the 'veined' rule C211. 'Several' is not a number, so the count pattern cannot hold it. What the word reliably says is that veins are present.

Appressed (FLOPO_0991064) is the defining content. Pressed flat against an upward-running axis already implies the erect direction, as the rule's own reason says. 'Erect' adds nothing, and there is no compound class.

'Bulged' means swollen or protruding, but not necessarily on one side. Gibbous (FLOPO_0991130) requires one-sided swelling, so it is too narrow. PATO swollen is already used for flora 'swollen' bases and nodes, as the accepted pairs in flora_union_pairs.tsv show.

Connivent (FLOPO_0991147) requires the parts to converge and touch. 'Converging' only says they lean toward each other, as stamens or follicles do. Neither PATO nor FLOPO has a convergent class, so no existing class fits.

A gummy bud, leaf or fruit surface is sticky with exudate, which is PATO viscid (PATO_0001370), a sticky coating. Resinous (FLOPO_0991075) would be wrong because gum is not resin. The kind of exudate is a chemical detail.

For veins, 'sharply defined' means distinct or clearly visible, which matches the existing reading of 'veins distinct' and 'vein visible' as conspicuous (PATO_0000463, R2040). For colour zones, margins and borders it means 'clearly delimited', which conspicuous does not cover. This mirrors R0594.

'Raised' is what prominent (PATO_0001482) means: standing out beyond a surface. This matches the accepted 'bulging' rule (R0021). 'Round' grades the form of the raised area, as 'low' does in low-conic. The shape can be added separately but is not needed for the rule.

An aril, calyx tube or pistil that is scarcely developed is reduced to a trace. Accepted rules read obsolete (C234), rudimentary (C142), obsolescent (R0690) and subnul (R0853/R1989) the same way, as vestigial (PATO_0000588).

A biparous cyme is a dichasium, and PO lists dichasium as a synonym of cyme inflorescence. The rule should become an entity-presence rule ('cyme inflorescence present'), the same as R0023 dichasial. Bifurcated (PATO_0001784) is wrong.

Chestnut-brown is an exact synonym of chestnut colour (PATO_0104329). 'Pale' is a lightness modifier, as in the accepted rule R1850 (light straw-colored maps to straw yellow). PATO has no pale chestnut class.
Hypocrepiform means horseshoe-shaped. It is not hypocrateriform, which is salverform (FLOPO_0991144). No horseshoe-shape class exists in PATO or FLOPO. It needs a new class or should be rejected.

PO gives midrib as an exact synonym of leaf midvein (PO_0020139), but that class is for leaves only. On sepals, bracts, glumes or valves the target should be vascular bundle (PO_0005020), and in mosses the costa (PO_0030072). The accepted rules for midvein (R1773) and midnerved (R1472) say the same.

Botanical 'nervous' (nervosus) means nerved. Accepted rules map its variants (nervate R0115, nervose R0478, nervured R1357) to vascular bundle present with no part constraint, and veins occur on stems and fruits as well as flat parts. 'Énerviées' (nerveless) belongs to the 'nerveless' rule.
